title: Social Sciences Research and SR&ED Eligibility | Canada FAQ
description: Research in the social sciences or the humanities is not eligible for Canada's SR&ED tax incentives. See what the rules exclude.
summary: Research in the social sciences or the humanities is not eligible for Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives. Paragraph (g) of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act excludes it, so Canadian claimants cannot earn SR&ED deductions or investment tax credits on such work, although psychological research can qualify as support work for eligible core SR&ED.

body.text: Research in the social sciences or the humanities is not eligible for Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives. Paragraph (g) of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act excludes it, so Canadian claimants cannot earn SR&ED deductions or investment tax credits on such work, although psychological research can qualify as support work for eligible core SR&ED.
Executive Overview and Legislative Architecture of the Canadian SR&ED Regime

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED Tax Incentive Program) represents the cornerstone of federal industrial and technological innovation policy, supporting more than 22,000 claimants nationwide, including roughly 4,000 enterprises operating within Quebec. Administered jointly through legislative policy established by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement conducted by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the program delivers statutory tax relief via two distinct, interlocking mechanisms under the Income Tax Act (Canada) (ITA): an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable deduction against net business income for allowable SR&ED expenditures pooled under section 37, and a refundable or non-refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated on qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsections 127(5) through 127(35) and section 127.1.

Between 2024 and 2026, the federal SR&ED framework underwent its most significant structural expansion since the 2012–2014 legislative contractions. In response to persistent business productivity gaps and heightened international tax competition, the Department of Finance initiated a two-phase public consultation process beginning on January 31, 2024, which examined program eligibility criteria, expenditure thresholds, intellectual property (IP) retention within Canada, and the feasibility of a preferential "patent box" regime. Following the initial consultation closure on April 15, 2024, the federal government tabled Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) on April 16, 2024, committing an initial $600 million over four years commencing in 2025 (and $150 million annually on an ongoing basis) and launching a second consultation phase from April 25, 2024, to May 27, 2024, focused on technical reforms and expanding access to the enhanced 35% credit rate for Canadian public companies.

Culminating in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) tabled on December 16, 2024, and subsequent legislative enactments reflected in Bill C-15 and the 2026 administrative revision cycle, the federal government expanded the fiscal commitment to $1.9 billion over six years. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024), the modernized architecture substantially raises the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC, elevates the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds, introduces an elective gross revenue phase-out structure, extends the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restores the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024. These reforms collectively realign Canada's innovation tax architecture to support scaling technology, manufacturing, and life sciences firms across the transition from private venture-backed growth to public capital markets.

body.text: Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Criteria
Analysis of Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The threshold question in every Canadian R&D tax audit is whether the underlying technical activities satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. The statute defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. To qualify, the systematic investigation or search must fall within one of four affirmative statutory paragraphs—paragraphs (a) through (d)—and must not fall within the seven statutory exclusions enumerated in paragraphs (e) through (k).

Under paragraph (a), eligible work encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (b), eligible work encompasses applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Under paragraph (c), eligible work encompasses experimental development, which is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The overwhelming majority of industrial and commercial SR&ED claims in Canada are filed under paragraph (c), as the statutory language explicitly encompasses incremental technological improvements alongside breakthrough innovations, provided the claimant seeks to advance the technological knowledge base rather than merely applying existing engineering routines.

Beyond core research and experimental development, paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1) extends eligibility to support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight specific, statutorily enumerated disciplines: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. Such work qualifies only where it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work under paragraph (d) cannot qualify as SR&ED on a standalone basis. Moreover, the statutory list of eight support categories is exhaustive, meaning that activities falling outside those eight categories cannot be claimed as support work even if they facilitate an R&D project. The dual statutory requirement that support work be "commensurate with the needs" and "directly in support" of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development operates as a structural safeguard that prevents claimants from sweeping general commercial software development, broad manufacturing runs, or over-scoped engineering design into an SR&ED project.
Statutory Exclusions and the Administrative Purpose Test

Paragraphs (e) through (k) of subsection 248(1) of the ITA explicitly exclude seven categories of activity from the definition of SR&ED. Specifically, the statute excludes market research or sales promotion under paragraph (e); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes under paragraph (f); research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph (g); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas under paragraph (h); the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph (i); style changes under paragraph (j); and routine data collection under paragraph (k). Collectively referred to in CRA guidance as the statutory exclusions, these activities cannot be claimed even when conducted within an innovative enterprise.

In the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, the CRA emphasizes that excluded work should only be evaluated after the reviewer has established whether core eligible work under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) has been performed. A single business operation may simultaneously conduct eligible SR&ED and statutorily excluded activities. For example, a mining enterprise may conduct eligible experimental development on a novel metallurgical extraction process while simultaneously prospecting for minerals; the eligible experimental development remains claimable, whereas the mineral prospecting must be carved out and excluded under paragraph (h).

When distinguishing between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "data collection" or "testing") and statutorily excluded work (such as "routine data collection" under paragraph (k) or "quality control or routine testing" under paragraph (f)), the determinative legal criterion is purpose. The auditor must determine why the activity was performed and whether it was carried out specifically to perform scientific research or experimental development or for some other commercial or operational reason. If data collection or testing is executed specifically to test a formulated hypothesis and resolve a technological uncertainty within an experimental development project, it qualifies as paragraph (d) support work because its purpose is directly tied to performing SR&ED. Conversely, if the identical testing or data collection protocol is performed to verify commercial compliance, calibrate standard equipment, or monitor commercial production output, it is excluded under paragraphs (f), (i), or (k).
The Five Judicial Criteria Versus the CRA Three-Criteria Administrative Framework

Canadian jurisprudence evaluates technical eligibility under the five-part legal framework articulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998) and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1999) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (at paragraph 17). Concurrently, the CRA’s administrative policy consolidates these five judicial inquiries into a three-criteria operational test—scientific or technological uncertainty, systematic investigation or search, and scientific or technological advancement—mapped directly onto Part 2, Section B of Form T661.

headers: Judicial Criterion (Northwest Hydraulic / C.W. Agencies, 2001 FCA 393)
Corresponding CRA Administrative Criterion & Form T661 Line

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?
Scientific or Technological Uncertainty (Form T661, Part 2, Section B, Line 242 — Max 350 words)

Existing design methods are inapplicable; specifications conflict with known standards; parameters lie outside normal operating ranges; or system-level interactions create unpredictable behaviour that standard practice cannot resolve.
2. Hypothesis Formulation: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Systematic Investigation or Search (Form T661, Part 2, Section B, Line 244 — Max 700 words)
Generation of an idea consistent with known scientific facts that serves as a starting point for investigation, expressed as a testable causal proposition rather than random trial-and-error.
3. Scientific Method Discipline: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
Systematic Investigation or Search (Form T661, Part 2, Section B, Line 244 — Max 700 words)

Controlled experimentation or mathematical/engineering analysis with a logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests, leading to logical conclusions based on observed results.
4. Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement?
Scientific or Technological Advancement (Form T661, Part 2, Section B, Line 246 — Max 350 words)

Generation of new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the claimant's and industry's technological knowledge base. Even a slight advancement or the conclusive rejection of a hypothesis qualifies, whereas acquiring existing know-how through training or hiring consultants does not.
5. Contemporaneous Record-Keeping: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?
Contemporaneous Documentation (Form T661, Part 2, Section C & Appendix 2; embedded in Systematic Investigation)
Evidence generated as the work progresses—such as test logs, prototypes, git commits, lab notebooks, and failure analyses—substantiating that a systematic investigation occurred.

body.text: A recurring compliance vulnerability arises when taxpayers conflate commercial or business objectives with genuine technological uncertainty. Under CRA audit guidelines and Tax Court jurisprudence, an internal lack of familiarity with an existing technology—or the need to acquire available knowledge or know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—does not satisfy the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement. Rather, the uncertainty must represent an objective capability gap in the underlying field of science or technology—evidenced by inapplicable design methods, conflicting specifications, excessive unknown variables, parameters outside normal operating ranges, or an evolving problem nature—such that competent professionals in the field cannot predict whether a given design or methodology will succeed without undertaking systematic experimentation or analysis.
Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and the 2024–2026 Reforms
Structural Evolution of the Federal Investment Tax Credit

The calculation of federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits under section 127 and section 127.1 of the ITA depends on three primary variables: the legal status and ownership control of the claimant, the timing of the claimant's taxation year relative to the December 16, 2024 effective date of the 2024 Fall Economic Statement reforms, and whether the underlying qualified expenditures are current or capital in nature.

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the enhanced 35% federal ITC was restricted exclusively to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, generating a maximum enhanced fully refundable credit of $1,050,000 per year on current expenditures. The $3,000,000 expenditure limit was subject to a straight-line reduction where the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and its associated corporations) fell between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, eliminating access to the 35% rate once taxable capital reached $50,000,000. Depending on whether a CCPC's income or taxable capital in the preceding taxation year remained within qualifying thresholds, current expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit earned the 15% general rate with 40% refundability. Conversely, all Canadian public corporations, foreign-controlled corporations, and large CCPCs exceeding the phase-out threshold were restricted to the 15% non-refundable general rate. Unincorporated businesses, individuals, and certain trusts benefited from a 15% ITC that was 40% refundable on qualified SR&ED expenditures.

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024), the federal government enacted four interconnected structural expansions to modernize the credit architecture and target high-growth-potential firms. First, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement raised the annual SR&ED expenditure limit on which the enhanced 35% ITC can be earned from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, enabling qualifying corporations to claim up to $1,575,000 per year in 100% refundable enhanced ITCs on current expenditures. Subsequent legislative enhancements for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, further increased this annual SR&ED expenditure limit from $4,500,000 to $6,000,000, expanding the maximum annual enhanced refundable credit to $2,100,000.

Second, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range for CCPCs was elevated from the historical $10,000,000 to $50,000,000 corridor to a widened corridor of $15,000,000 to $75,000,000. Consequently, a CCPC retains its full expenditure limit until prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, and retains partial access to the 35% enhanced rate until taxable capital reaches $75,000,000.

Third, to prevent innovative Canadian enterprises from losing access to refundable R&D support upon executing an initial public offering (IPO) or listing on a stock exchange, the reforms extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on up to $4,500,000 (and $6,000,000 under the expanded threshold) of qualifying SR&ED expenditures annually, with a 15% non-refundable credit applying to excess expenditures. To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must satisfy three statutory conditions throughout the taxation year: it must be resident in Canada; it must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or have validly elected (or been designated) to be a public corporation for purposes of the ITA; and it must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Canadian corporations that are controlled by non-residents remain excluded from the enhanced rate and continue to be limited to the 15% non-refundable tax credit.

Fourth, for an ECPC (and its corporate group, where applicable), the annual expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when the corporation's average gross revenue over the three preceding taxation years falls between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000. Crucially, the legislation grants CCPCs an annual election to have their expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% credit determined based on this same three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure instead of using the taxable capital structure. This dual-track elective mechanism allows each CCPC to select whichever metric provides the more advantageous expenditure limit, delivering substantial cash-flow relief to capital-intensive, pre-revenue, or early-commercialization CCPCs—such as biotechnology, life sciences, clean technology, and hardware firms—whose balance-sheet equity or debt exceeds $15,000,000 in taxable capital but whose three-year average gross revenue remains below $15,000,000.

The mathematical formula for the expenditure limit (E) under the post-December 15, 2024 regime—where L represents the applicable statutory cap ($4,500,000 under FES 2024 or $6,000,000 under the expanded threshold) and X represents either prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (for non-electing CCPCs) or three-year average gross revenue (for ECPCs and electing CCPCs)—is expressed as follows:
E = L × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if X does not exceed $15,000,000, and otherwise is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which X exceeds $15,000,000.

body.text: Carryforward, Carryback, and Federal Tax Offset Mechanics

Where an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit is non-refundable (or only partially refundable at 40%), the credit is first applied under subsection 127(5) of the ITA to reduce the taxpayer's federal Part I income tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Any unused non-refundable federal SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years to reduce federal taxes payable in those prior periods, or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset future federal tax liabilities.

Importantly, the utilization of an SR&ED ITC—whether through an offset against Part I tax payable or through receipt of a cash refund under section 127.1—triggers a corresponding reduction in the taxpayer's section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the subsequent taxation year pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA. If the taxpayer has already deducted the full section 37 pool in the prior year so that the pool reduction creates a negative balance, that negative balance is included in the taxpayer's taxable income in the subsequent taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA. This statutory inclusion mechanism prevents a double tax benefit—deducting the same dollar of tax credit that was refunded or used to pay tax—while still affording the claimant a one-year timing deferral on the taxability of the credit.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methodologies, and Capital Expenditure Reinstatement
Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, and the 10% Foreign Work Allowance

Salaries and wages represent the largest expenditure component within the Canadian SR&ED program. Under section 37 and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a claimant may include the portion of salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Direct engagement encompasses hands-on experimentation, engineering analysis, prototype fabrication, eligible paragraph (d) support work, and direct first-line technical supervision of SR&ED personnel. Administrative, clerical, legal, human resources, and executive management activities not directly involved in technical R&D execution are excluded under the Proxy Method, and may only be captured under the Traditional Method to the strict extent they are proven to be directly attributable and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED.

Three statutory restrictions govern the calculation of eligible SR&ED salaries and wages. First, the ITA imposes strict caps on "specified employees"—defined in subsection 248(1) as employees who do not deal at arm's length with the employer or who are specified shareholders owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation. For specified employees (including incorporated medical or professional practitioners where applicable), the statute prohibits claiming any bonus or remuneration based on profits or income, requiring claimants to distinguish fixed base wages from profit-linked bonuses. Furthermore, total claimable SR&ED salary and wages for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for direct expenditure pool purposes, and cannot exceed 2.5 times the YMPE (prorated for the number of days employed in the year) when computing the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661.

Second, pursuant to subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any salary, wages, or other remuneration accrued in a taxation year that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of that taxation year is statutorily deemed not to have been incurred in the taxation year. Instead, the unpaid remuneration is deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid, and both unpaid current-year amounts and paid prior-year amounts must be tracked on the corresponding adjustment lines of Part 3 and Part 4 of Form T661.

Third, while core SR&ED must generally be undertaken within Canada (which, under subsection 37(1.3) of the ITA, includes Canada's exclusive economic zone), subsection 37(1.4) and subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA provide a limited foreign salary allowance. Specifically, a claimant may include salaries and wages paid to Canadian-resident employees for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada, provided that the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer rather than subcontracted, is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer, and is capped at a maximum of 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year.
Materials Consumed and Transformed

Allowable SR&ED expenditures include the cost of materials that are either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed encompass items that are destroyed, rendered virtually valueless, or exhausted during experimental testing, laboratory trials, or prototype validation, such as chemical reagents, destructive testing coupons, or sacrificial substrates. Materials transformed encompass raw materials or components that are physically integrated or modified into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig during the R&D process, where the resulting body or item retains some potential commercial or scrap value. Materials incorporated directly into commercial products sold in the ordinary course without experimental uncertainty do not qualify.

If materials transformed in SR&ED (or an experimental production run) are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, statutory recapture rules require the claimant to reduce the SR&ED expenditure pool and repay or offset the associated ITC attributable to the lower of the cost of the materials or the fair market value or proceeds of disposition. However, as confirmed by Tax Court jurisprudence, the subsequent commercial sale of experimental production does not disqualify the underlying SR&ED labour and overhead incurred during the experimental run, provided SR&ED was genuinely performed and the primary purpose of the work at the time of execution was to resolve technological uncertainty.
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Non-Arm's Length Transfers

Where a claimant engages an arm's-length Canadian contractor to perform SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf (comprising paragraph (c) experimental development or paragraph (d) support work where the claimant controls the specifications and retains rights to exploit the results), the expenditure is deductible at 100% under section 37, but only 80% of the contract payment qualifies as a "qualified expenditure" for Investment Tax Credit purposes under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. This 20% statutory reduction removes the presumed profit markup of the arm's-length contractor. Similarly, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D consortia—which are reported on Schedule A and Part 3 of Form T661—are subject to the 80% ITC inclusion rule. Payments made to foreign subcontractors performing work outside Canada are completely ineligible for SR&ED deductions or ITCs.

Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's length party, payments under the contract do not directly qualify as SR&ED expenditures in the hands of the payer, and an expenditure incurred for the benefit of a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier in respect of the expenditure is similarly restricted. Instead, the non-arm's length performer incurs the underlying qualified expenditures (wages, materials, overhead) reported via Schedule C / Part 3 of Form T661, and the parties may jointly execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the qualified expenditures to the payer. Under the 2026 revision of Form T1146, the qualified expenditures transferred on Line 010 must be explicitly broken down between current expenditures on Line 015 and capital expenditures on Line 020 so that each category is reported in the proper column of Form T661 for both the transferor and the transferee.
Overhead Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Versus Traditional Method

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, every claimant must elect annually whether to compute SR&ED overhead using the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method; once the return is filed for the taxation year, this election is binding and irrevocable for that year. Under the Proxy Method, overhead and other indirect expenditures are represented by a notional formula—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) computed in Part 5 of Form T661 at 55% of the eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada—eliminating the need to track and allocate itemized overhead expenses. Because the PPA is a notional calculation, it is not deducted in the section 37 SR&ED pool (underlying overhead costs are deducted as ordinary business expenses), but flows from Part 5 directly onto Line 502 in Part 4 of Form T661 to earn SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant enters "0" for the PPA and instead specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates all overhead and other expenditures that are directly attributable and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, subject to the exclusions for prescribed expenditures in section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations. While the Traditional Method can yield a higher credit ceiling for facility-heavy industrial projects, it imposes a substantially higher documentation and audit burden than the Proxy Method preferred by software and technology companies.

cells: Statutory & Regulatory Basis
Subsection 127(9) ITA ("prescribed proxy amount") and Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations.
Section 37 ITA, Subsection 127(9) ITA, and Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations.
Overhead Calculation Formula

Notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base (subject to 2.5x YMPE cap for specified employees and excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, and s. 78(4) unpaid wages).
Actual overhead and other expenditures specifically identified, tracked, and proven to be directly attributable (and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.
Treatment in Section 37 Deduction Pool
PPA is not added to the section 37 SR&ED deduction pool; underlying overhead expenses are deducted under ordinary business expense rules (sections 9 and 18 ITA).
Directly attributable overhead is included directly in the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.
Treatment in Part 4 Qualified Expenditure Pool (ITC)
The 55% PPA is added directly on Line 502 of Part 4 of Form T661 to generate federal and provincial SR&ED ITCs.
Itemized overhead flows from Part 3 into Part 4 to generate federal and provincial SR&ED ITCs.
Audit & Documentation Burden
Low overhead audit friction; CRA verifies only the directly engaged SR&ED salary base and time-tracking allocations.
High audit friction; claimant must substantiate causal link and incremental allocation of every overhead invoice, utility bill, and support salary.
Optimal Claimant Profile
Software, AI, engineering, biotechnology, and labour-intensive R&D enterprises where direct salaries represent the dominant cost driver.
Heavy industrial, manufacturing, or energy operations with massive consumable shop utilities, dedicated facility overheads, and low direct labour ratios.

body.text: Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

One of the most consequential reforms introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement—and operationalized in the 2026 version of Form T661 following the enactment of Bill C-15—is the restoration of capital expenditures and capital lease costs to full SR&ED eligibility, reversing the 2014 repeal (enacted in 2012) that had excluded capital assets for over a decade. The reinstated capital expenditure rules apply to depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), and, in the case of lease costs, to amounts that first become payable after December 15, 2024. Capital expenditures made before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible for SR&ED.

Under the restored rules—which generally mirror the statutory architecture that existed prior to 2014—expenditures incurred to acquire new or used depreciable property qualify for both immediate 100% income deduction against income under section 37 and SR&ED Investment Tax Credits under section 127 if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intends that the property will either be used all or substantially all (defined as 90% or more) of the operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or have all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value consumed in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. In addition, the 2026 version of Form T661 introduces dedicated parts to report these capital expenditures as well as expenditures on shared-use equipment (SUE), ensuring that current and capital amounts are reported in separate columns and flow independently into the qualified expenditure and investment tax credit calculations.

Two critical compliance rules govern post-December 15, 2024 SR&ED capital expenditures and create ongoing audit considerations under Bill C-15. First, differential refundability applies: while a qualifying CCPC or ECPC earns a 100% cash refund on ITCs computed at the 35% enhanced rate on current expenditures, ITCs computed at the 35% enhanced rate on capital expenditures are only 40% refundable, matching the 40% refundability rate applicable to ITCs computed at the 15% general rate for qualified corporations. Second, if a taxpayer subsequently sells or converts the use of SR&ED capital property to commercial operations, statutory recapture rules designed to recover previously claimed tax benefits apply. These recapture provisions affect both the capital cost allowance claimed and unclaimed SR&ED capital expenditures, as well as the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit.
Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

To prevent taxpayers from earning SR&ED tax credits on expenditures funded by public subsidies or third-party commercial reimbursements, subsection 127(18) of the ITA mandates that the pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures be reduced by all government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED. Government assistance encompasses federal, provincial, or municipal grants, subsidies, forgivable loans (such as National Research Council Assist or innovation contributions), and provincial R&D tax credits.

Where persons not dealing at arm's length collaborate on SR&ED and allocate government or non-government assistance between themselves, they must execute Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). Under the 2026 revision of Form T1145, the assistance allocated on Line 010 is broken down between current expenditures on Line 015 and capital expenditures on Line 020, ensuring that each amount is reported in the correct column of the transferee's Form T661. Conversely, where a claimant repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool, the repayment is added back to the pool in the year of repayment via Schedule B and Part 3/Part 4 of Form T661.
Complementary Federal Tax Incentives, Accelerated Depreciation, and Direct Innovation Funding

Beyond the SR&ED program, Canadian tax law and federal industrial policy between 2024 and 2026 deployed a suite of accelerated capital cost allowance (CCA) incentives, clean economy investment tax credits, intellectual property consultations, and sovereign artificial intelligence (AI) funding programs that interact directly with corporate R&D planning.
Accelerated Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) and Immediate Expensing Regimes

To address Canada's historical productivity gap and incentivize capital investment in innovation-enabling assets, Budget 2024 introduced an immediate 100% first-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) deduction for eligible productivity-enhancing property acquired on or after April 16, 2024, that becomes available for use before January 1, 2027. This 100% immediate write-off applies to patents and rights to use patented information (CCA Class 44), data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software (CCA Class 46), and general-purpose electronic data processing equipment, computers, and related systems software (CCA Class 50). Eligible property in these classes that becomes available for use during calendar year 2027 continues to benefit from the existing Accelerated Investment Incentive.

Expanding upon these targeted capital write-offs, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement proposed the full reinstatement of the general Accelerated Investment Incentive for qualifying depreciable capital property, allowing businesses to claim up to three times the normal first-year CCA for eligible property acquired on or after January 1, 2025, that becomes available for use before 2030, followed by a gradual phase-out starting in 2030 and full elimination for property becoming available after 2033. Simultaneously, FES 2024 proposed to fully reinstate 100% immediate expensing in the year of acquisition—on the same 2025 to 2033 phase-out schedule—for manufacturing or processing machinery and equipment (CCA Class 53), clean energy generation and energy conservation equipment (CCA Classes 43.1 and 43.2), and zero-emission vehicles. Additionally, to encourage entrepreneurial capital recycling into innovative ventures, FES 2024 enhanced the eligible small business corporation (ESBC) share capital gains rollover effective January 1, 2025, expanding the replacement share acquisition window to include the entire calendar year following the year of disposition, expanding eligible ESBC shares to include both common and preferred shares, and doubling the carrying value limit of the assets of the ESBC and related corporations from $50 million to $100 million.
Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits (Bill C-59 and Budget 2024 Enhancements)

To anchor industrial decarbonization and critical mineral processing, the federal government reaffirmed and legislated five major Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits: the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) ITC; the Clean Technology ITC; the Clean Hydrogen ITC; the Clean Electricity ITC; and the Clean Technology Manufacturing (CTM) ITC. While Bill C-59 enacted the CCUS and Clean Technology ITCs alongside labour requirements and partnership rules in mid-2024, separate legislation introduced in Parliament in May 2024 and refined in Budget 2024 codified the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC.

The Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC provides a 30% refundable tax credit on the cost of investments in eligible property used all or substantially all for eligible clean technology manufacturing or "qualifying mineral activities" that produce six qualifying critical materials: copper, nickel, cobalt, lithium, graphite, and rare earth elements. Qualifying mineral activities cover extraction, processing activities at mine or well sites, tailing ponds, mills, smelters, or refineries, recycling activities, and specific graphite activities. Recognizing that critical mineral production frequently occurs in polymetallic projects yielding multiple metals simultaneously, Budget 2024 modified the CTM ITC rules effective for property acquired on or after January 1, 2024, so that the financial value of qualifying materials is used to assess property usage, and expanded eligible expenditures to cover property used in qualifying mineral activities at mine or well sites (including tailing ponds) expected to produce primarily—meaning 50% or more of the financial value of the output—qualifying critical materials. To substantiate CTM ITC claims under this rule, claimants must submit a formal attestation from an arm's-length qualified engineer or geoscientist to the CRA for each relevant mine or well site, while a statutory safe-harbour rule calculates critical mineral proportions using a five-year historical average value to mitigate commodity price volatility under the ITC recapture mechanism.
Direct Innovation Funding, Sovereign AI Strategy, and Intellectual Property Initiatives

Canada supplements tax-based incentives with substantial direct R&D funding programs and regulatory modernization. Having invested over $16 billion since 2016 to support scientific discovery and research talent—including the $2 billion Global Innovation Clusters program and the $3.5 billion Sustainable Canadian Agricultural Partnership running through 2028—Budget 2024 proposed $2.4 billion in new Artificial Intelligence investments to build upon the Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy launched in 2017. This $2.4 billion AI package comprises $2.0 billion to launch the AI Compute Access Fund and the Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy to expand domestic computing capacity; $200 million to accelerate AI adoption in key sectors and assist AI startups in commercializing new technologies; $100 million for the National Research Council's (NRC) AI Assist Program to support Canadian SMEs in building and deploying AI solutions; and $50 million to support workers in sectors impacted by AI, alongside establishing the AI Safety Institute of Canada and enforcing the proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act.

In parallel with the public consultation on creating a federal "patent box" regime (which closed its initial phase on April 15, 2024), Budget 2024 committed $14.5 million over two years for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Innovation Asset Collective to assist SMEs in intellectual property creation and retention. Furthermore, the federal government announced amendments to the Red Tape Reduction Act to broaden the use of regulatory sandboxes—enabling temporary rules for testing novel products, services, and regulatory approaches—and partnered with Talent for Innovation Canada to launch a pilot initiative training R&D talent in biomanufacturing, clean technology, electric vehicle manufacturing, and microelectronics. When stacking direct grants such as the NRC AI Assist Program with SR&ED claims, claimants must account for the statutory assistance reduction rule in Part 4 of Form T661, whereas non-overlapping patent strategies must also account for evolving Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO) guidelines on computer-implemented inventions, medical treatments, and plant varieties.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Canadian provinces and the Yukon Territory maintain complementary R&D tax credit regimes that harmonize with the federal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. In Ontario, the CRA administers both the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) and the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC). The OITC provides an 8% refundable tax credit for small and medium-sized companies on eligible Ontario R&D expenditures up to $3,000,000, phasing out on prior-year taxable capital and taxable income (while a March 28, 2018 provincial budget proposal had proposed scaling the OITC up to 12% where the ratio of Ontario R&D expenditures to gross revenues reached 20% or more, subject to a 90% prior-year R&D spending maintenance rule, the baseline 8% OITC rate remains the foundational SME benchmark alongside the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC).

In Quebec, where SR&ED tax incentives support approximately 4,000 companies, provincial R&D tax credits are administered independently by Revenu Québec rather than the CRA. Notably, in its recent fiscal reviews, the Quebec provincial government elected to preserve the financial vitality of its R&D tax credit architecture rather than draining the SR&ED program to meet its broader provincial target of achieving $2.9 billion in total savings over five years. Because all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, any provincial credit earned on current-year SR&ED expenditures reduces the federal pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661 before the federal ITC (at 35% or 15%) is computed.

body.text: Administrative Governance, Filing Procedures, and Form T661 Line-by-Line Compliance
Governing Authorities and the Dual-Stream CRA Audit Process

The federal SR&ED program is governed through a coordinated administrative model in which the Department of Finance Canada establishes statutory policy and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) executes compliance, risk assessment, and technical/financial verification through specialized SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs). When a claimant files Form T661, the CRA utilizes Part 2 project descriptions to conduct an initial review aimed at establishing, with reasonable confidence, whether the claimed work meets SR&ED eligibility requirements so that low-risk claims can be expedited and processed in a timely manner. Where further verification is required, the CRA conducts a dual-stream review in which a Research and Technology Advisor evaluates technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) of the ITA while a Financial Reviewer audits expenditure pools, proxy salary bases, and supporting accounting documentation. Claimants and preparers also actively engage with CRA administrative processes regarding pre-claim approval/consultation mechanisms, Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) requests for audit working papers, processing service standards, and Notices of Objection.
Statutory Filing Deadlines and the Strict 18-Month Corporate Bar

Under the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy and the ITA, a claimant must file Form T661 containing all prescribed information, together with the applicable investment tax credit schedule, within 12 months after the filing due date of the claimant's income tax return for the taxation year. For a corporation, the T2 corporate income tax return filing due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, meaning the corporation has an absolute statutory deadline of 18 months after the end of its taxation year to file or amend prescribed information in respect of an expenditure on Form T661 and to include the ITC amount on Schedule T2SCH31. For example, a corporation with a March 31, 2022 taxation year-end had a T2 filing due date of September 30, 2022, and had until September 30, 2023, to file or amend its Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31.

For an individual (sole proprietorship), Form T661 and Form T2038(IND) constitute part of the individual's T1 Income Tax and Benefit Return, which has a filing due date of June 15 of the following calendar year, yielding an SR&ED reporting deadline of June 15 of the second following year. For a trust, Form T661 and Form T2038(IND) must be filed with the T3 Trust Income Tax and Information Return within 12 months of the trust's T3 filing due date (which is 90 days after the trust's year-end). Partnerships must follow the specialized partnership filing instructions in Guide T4088.

This 12-month post-filing-due-date reporting deadline is strictly enforced: failure to report an expenditure on the appropriate line of Form T661 by the SR&ED reporting deadline permanently bars the expenditure from being added to the pool or earning an ITC. However, two items are explicitly exempt from the SR&ED reporting deadline: first, the deduction of an amount from the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is not subject to the deadline provided the expenditures comprising the pool were identified on time on Form T661; second, the claim preparer information in Part 9 of Form T661 is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline, and missing, incomplete, or inaccurate Part 9 information will not cause the SR&ED claim to be disallowed, though it triggers a statutory $1,000 penalty. Claimants using tax preparation software to transmit Form T661 electronically must not submit duplicate paper copies of Form T661.
Exhaustive Line-by-Line Audit Breakdown of Form T661 (Including 2026 Revisions)

Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and its companion Guide T4088 organize prescribed compliance information across 10 mandatory parts and two appendices, which were updated in the 2026 form version to incorporate separate columns and parts for post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures and shared-use equipment:

cells: Part 1 — General Information

Line 010 (Name of claimant), Tax year start/end dates, 15-character Business Number (BN), Line 050 (Number of projects), Lines 100–110 (Financial contact name, phone, fax), Lines 115–125 (Technical contact name, phone, fax), Lines 151–157 (Partnership information).

Establishes the administrative header, total project count, and designated internal personnel best suited to provide supporting financial and technical information during a CRA review. Round all dollar amounts on the form to the nearest dollar.
Part 2 — Project Information (Section A: Project Identification)
Project title, internal code, start and end dates, Field of Science or Technology classification code (from Appendix 1), continuation indicator, and joint/collaborative project disclosure.

A separate complete Part 2 is required for each project claimed. Claimants with more than 20 projects may choose to submit Part 2 at filing for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, but must complete and maintain at their place of business a Part 2 for every project claimed and submit them upon CRA request, failing which the project's expenditures are disallowed.
Part 2 — Project Information (Section B: Project Descriptions)

Line 242 (Scientific or technological uncertainties attempted to overcome — Max 350 words) Line 244 (Work performed in the tax year to overcome uncertainties — Max 700 words) Line 246 (Scientific or technological advancements achieved — Max 350 words).

Establishes how the project meets the statutory definition of SR&ED. Must be prepared by or with personnel familiar with the scientific or technical content, using clear, concise technical facts within the strict word limits.
Part 2 — Project Information (Section C: Additional Project Information)

Line 253 (Employee directly involved in the project), Line 254 (Name), Line 255 (Other employee of the company), preparer qualifications, foreign work indicator, subcontractors, and supporting documentation checklist (Appendix 2).

Identifies key technical personnel (up to three per project), discloses whether work was performed outside Canada or by subcontractors, and catalogues the contemporaneous evidence maintained to substantiate the work.
Part 3 — Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures (Sections A, B, and C + 2026 Capital Parts)

Section A: Select method (Proxy vs. Traditional) to calculate SR&ED expenditures. Section B: Calculation of allowable SR&ED expenditures (materials transformed, materials consumed, s. 78(4) unpaid/paid adjustments, directly engaged salaries/wages, third-party payments on Schedule A, special situations on Schedule B, non-arm's length transactions on Schedule C, plus 2026 capital expenditure and shared-use equipment parts). Section C: Calculation of pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.

The election between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method in Section A is binding for the taxation year. Under the 2026 version of Form T661, current expenditures and post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures are reported in separate columns and flow independently into the expenditure pool and ITC calculations.
Part 4 — Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes

Line 492, Line 502 (Prescribed Proxy Amount from Part 5), Line 528 (Prescribed expenditures under Reg. 2902), Lines 552 & 554, plus adjustments for assistance (Form T1145) and non-arm's length transfers (Form T1146) in dual current/capital columns.
Computes the net qualified SR&ED expenditures used to calculate refundable and/or non-refundable ITCs on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND).
Part 5 — Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)
Section A: Salary base of directly engaged employees (subject to 2.5x YMPE cap for specified employees). Section B: Calculation of the 55% PPA notional overhead amount.
Completed only if the claimant elected the Proxy Method (enter "0" if using the Traditional Method). The resulting PPA is transferred to Line 502 in Part 4.
Part 6 — Project Costs
Project-by-project allocation of salaries/wages, materials, and subcontractor costs.

Must be completed at filing for all SR&ED projects claimed in the year (even where Part 2 narratives are submitted for only the 20 largest projects). Expenditures must be recorded and allocated on a project basis.
Part 7 — Additional Information
Statistical data on R&D funding sources and technological categories.
Mandatory statistical disclosure section.
Part 8 — Claim Checklist
Verification checklist confirming current form version, election indicator, retained supporting documents, and attached schedules.
Internal completeness check; skipping fields or leaving items uncorroborated increases the probability of audit selection.
Part 9 — Claim Preparer Information
Mandatory disclosure of every claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim, including billing arrangement (contingency, flat, hourly) and fees.

Added in 2013. A $1,000 penalty may be assessed if prescribed information on preparers and billing arrangements is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, for which the claimant and claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable.
Part 10 — Certification
Name and signature of authorized signing officer of the corporation (or individual) and name of the person/firm who completed the form.
Attests to the accuracy and completeness of the entire SR&ED claim.

body.text: Engineering Defensible Technical Narratives in Part 2, Section B (Lines 242, 244, and 246)

An SR&ED project comprises a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties in an attempt to achieve specific scientific or technological advancements through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals. Because the CRA determines project eligibility at the level necessary to recognize all work required for the attempted advancement (including support work), descriptions in Part 2, Section B that are vague, unnecessarily lengthy, or written in commercial rather than technical terms substantially increase the likelihood of a full audit review.

On Line 242 (What scientific or technological uncertainties did you attempt to overcome? — Maximum 350 words), the claimant must state what was scientifically or technologically unknown or unachievable at the outset of the project rather than describing a business or market problem. Strong Line 242 narratives specify quantitative technical metrics, physical or architectural constraints, and performance thresholds, explaining precisely why existing design methods, standard engineering procedures, or publicly available tools were insufficient to resolve the system or component uncertainty.

On Line 244 (What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the technological obstacles/uncertainties described in Line 242? — Maximum 700 words), the claimant must demonstrate that its methodology adhered to a structured, systematic investigation rather than ad hoc trial-and-error. In chronological order for the taxation year, Line 244 must explicitly describe the hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainties, the controlled experiments, prototypes, or engineering analyses conducted to test those hypotheses, the specific quantitative results obtained, and the logical conclusions drawn that guided subsequent iterations.

On Line 246 (What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244? — Maximum 350 words), the claimant must articulate the new technical knowledge generated that advances the technological knowledge base relative to publicly available industry knowledge. Even an incremental advancement—or knowledge gained from failed experiments proving why a hypothesized technical pathway cannot work under specified boundary conditions—qualifies, provided Line 246 connects the new knowledge directly back to the technological uncertainty defined in Line 242 rather than merely asserting that a commercial product or faster system was built.
Judicial Precedents, Contemporaneous Documentation, and CRA Audit Defence
Evolution of Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence Through November 2026

Canadian tax courts have established a rigorous body of precedent governing SR&ED eligibility, evidentiary burdens, and audit procedure. In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998), Justice Bowman formulated the five-part judicial test for SR&ED, which was subsequently affirmed and codified by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1999) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (at paragraph 17).

In National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47, the Tax Court of Canada evaluated software claims where the claimant attempted to use section variables, cookies, and temporary hidden browser-level data storage to make processing appear instantaneous after internet searches revealed no existing off-the-shelf solution. Reviewing the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion—whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed—the Court noted that while neither the ITA nor the Regulations explicitly mandate documentary evidence and oral testimonial evidence is legally permissible under RIS-Christie (paras. 14–15), failing to maintain adequate contemporaneous documentation carries severe litigation risk. Although the claimant's witness testified that he took contemporaneous notes and presented a Project Timeline detailing activities and hours, the Court held that it could not find a "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests," concluding that the claimant failed to prove a systematic investigation.

This evidentiary standard was reinforced by the Federal Court of Appeal on October 21, 2026, in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175, which upheld the Tax Court of Canada's decision in Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 183. The appellant had claimed SR&ED deductions and ITCs for 14 fish-cutting and recipe projects across its 2005 through 2009 taxation years; following an audit, the Minister disallowed 13 of the projects. For each of the 13 disputed projects, the Tax Court found factual shortcomings across multiple Northwest Hydraulic criteria: there was no formulated hypothesis, the work utilized existing technology and processes, the approach was trial-and-error rather than systematic investigation, records were inadequate, and the company had not established a gap in the industry's knowledge. On appeal, the company argued that the Tax Court had found its sole witness credible, that the witness had explained the project methodology and industry novelty, and that the Crown had neither displaced that testimony on cross-examination nor called a contradicting witness. Dismissing the appeal with costs, the Federal Court of Appeal drew a fundamental legal distinction between witness credibility and evidentiary sufficiency: believing a witness does not mean that the witness's evidence answers and demolishes the Minister's factual assumptions. Because the taxpayer bears the initial burden of establishing a prima facie case that refutes the Minister's assumption that no systematic investigation was undertaken to overcome technological uncertainty, credible and uncontradicted testimony describing trial-and-error work fails as a matter of law.

In Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7, the Tax Court of Canada issued a split decision in an industrial control systems appeal that contrasted a Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) software upgrade against the development of a Safety Integrity Level 4 (SIL 4) train-control box, while also adjudicating proxy wage calculation disputes. The decision underscores that routine SCADA software upgrades fail the technological uncertainty threshold, whereas safety-critical SIL 4 engineering involving complex system-level constraints qualifies, and reinforces that proxy wage allocations require a reasonable, verifiable basis.

Across broader Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal decisions reviewed in 2026, the courts have enforced strict boundaries on both taxpayers and the Crown. Where a claimant submitted 2006 and 2009 SR&ED technical reports containing plagiarized supplier and website text, the Tax Court held that copied technical write-ups constitute a misrepresentation that reopens statute-barred taxation years and supports penalties. Similarly, claims involving mobile direct-contact water heaters for hydraulic fracturing and roller-compacted concrete field processes were dismissed where field adjustments amounted to trial-and-error prototyping with vague hypotheses, known variables, reconstructed narratives, and employee wages that were estimated and split evenly across batches rather than substantiated contemporaneously. Conversely, taxpayers prevailed where expert testimony established system-level technological advancement in precision machining, where materials and experimental production were subsequently sold (confirming that SR&ED labour remains eligible despite a subsequent commercial sale, while materials sold are subject to ITC recapture), and where legal privilege was asserted over tax due-diligence reports (2026 TCC 185, holding that a due-diligence report and substantive emails prepared by Ernst & Young under a direct retainer from tax counsel were protected by solicitor-client privilege, whereas bare delivery emails were not, contrasted with 2026 FCA 147, where an accounting firm was ordered to comply with a CRA audit requirement it had resisted for seven years).

body.text: Contemporaneous Documentation Architecture for CRA Audit Defence

To satisfy the fifth criterion of C.W. Agencies and avoid the evidentiary shortfalls that proved fatal in National R&D and Tuna Temple, claimants must implement systematic, contemporaneous record-keeping protocols generated as the R&D progresses rather than reconstructing narratives years later during an audit. On the technical side—corresponding to Part 2, Section C and Appendix 2 of Form T661—claimants should preserve dated design documents identifying why existing engineering methods or standards were inapplicable, written hypotheses formulated prior to testing, version-controlled source code repositories, test logs and failure analyses demonstrating the logical progression from each experiment to subsequent hypothesis modifications, and quantitative records of the resulting technological advancement. Where AI tools are utilized by R&D performers or claim preparers, enterprises must never copy boilerplate supplier or external website text into Form T661 narratives, as plagiarized descriptions expose the claimant to statute-barred reassessments and gross negligence penalties.

On the financial side—corresponding to Parts 3 through 6 of Form T661—claimants must maintain project-level accounting ledgers and contemporaneous time-tracking records that substantiate the exact percentage of each employee's time directly engaged in eligible SR&ED versus non-SR&ED commercial activities, rather than estimating or splitting wages evenly across batches at year-end. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, claimants acquiring depreciable capital property or shared-use equipment must maintain acquisition invoices, commissioning records, and operating-time logs proving that the asset satisfies the 90% ("all or substantially all") SR&ED usage or value-consumption threshold and enabling accurate dual-column reporting across the 2026 versions of Form T661, Form T1145, and Form T1146.
Strategic Synthesis and Compliance Imperatives for Canadian Claimants

The 2024–2026 legislative modernization of Canada's R&D tax incentive landscape substantially enhances the value and accessibility of the SR&ED program while heightening the technical precision required for tax compliance. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations should model both the expanded taxable capital phase-out corridor ($15 million to $75 million) and the new elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure to maximize access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC on up to $4.5 million (and $6.0 million under expanded thresholds) of qualified expenditures. Simultaneously, Canadian-resident public companies that are not controlled by non-residents should verify their qualification as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) to transition from the 15% non-refundable rate to the 35% enhanced refundable regime.

When planning capital investments acquired after December 15, 2024, tax directors must carefully weigh claiming reinstated SR&ED capital expenditure deductions and ITCs (which carry a 40% refundability rate on the 35% credit and remain subject to statutory recapture upon commercial conversion or sale) against alternative capital incentives, including the 100% immediate CCA expensing for patents, data network infrastructure, and computing equipment acquired between April 16, 2024, and January 1, 2027 (Classes 44, 46, and 50), the reinstated 100% immediate expensing for Class 53 manufacturing and processing machinery (2025–2033), and the 30% refundable Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC. Finally, in light of the Federal Court of Appeal's October 2026 ruling in Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175, claimants must recognize that witness credibility at trial cannot substitute for objective, contemporaneous proof of hypothesis formulation, controlled systematic experimentation, and a verified industry knowledge gap, making disciplined engineering documentation and timely filing within the strict 18-month statutory deadline the paramount imperatives of Canadian R&D tax management.
